transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi… yeah. I guess the main reason is my sleep. It’s gotten really unreliable lately. Like, I’ll be completely exhausted and get into bed thinking I should just pass out, but then my mind starts going over sales forecasts, team issues, little conversations from the day… and suddenly it’s been hours.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’m waking up around 3 or 4 in the morning and I can’t get my brain to shut off again. It’s frustrating because I’ll start thinking, “Okay, if I don’t sleep now tomorrow’s going to be a mess,” and then of course that makes it worse. I actually bought one of those new pillows—my sister swore by it—but it’s not really the pillow. It’s like my head won’t power down.
Do you find yourself feeling excessively worried or anxious during the day, even when you’re not trying to sleep?

Yeah… during the day too. It’s not just bedtime. Most days my mind kind of jumps around from one worry to the next—like whether we’re going to hit the launch numbers, or if someone on my team is unhappy and might leave, or the mortgage, or whether a client renewal is going to fall apart.

And it’s like, a small delay happens—someone doesn’t answer an email for a few hours—and my brain turns it into this whole bigger thing. I know some of it is probably normal work stress, I mean sales is always a little chaotic, but it feels like I can’t just let things be small.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, sad, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even when things aren’t particularly stressful at work?

I’m not sure… I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m sad exactly. It’s more like I get worn out, if that makes sense. Like after a long day I’ll think, “I should go meet friends,” and then I start thinking about parking, what time I’d have to leave, whether I’ll be tired tomorrow… and then I just don’t go.

But I don’t know if that’s losing interest or just being tired. I still like the things I like. I haven’t really thought of it as feeling down, I guess.
Have you noticed that things you used to look forward to, like hobbies or time with friends, don’t feel as enjoyable lately—even if you’re not stressed?

I don’t know if I’d say they don’t feel enjoyable. Like… if I’m actually there with my friends, I usually do have a good time. It’s more the getting myself to go that becomes this whole production in my head.

I used to do this Thursday trivia thing with a couple coworkers, and I still like it, but then I’ll start thinking about how late it’ll go, whether I’ll be dragging the next day, if I should answer emails first… and then I’m already kind of tired before I’ve even left. So I’m not sure if that’s the same thing as not enjoying it.

I guess I haven’t really noticed that things feel flat, exactly. It’s more like I talk myself out of them.
When you're actually doing things you used to enjoy, like the trivia night or time with friends, do you still feel the same sense of pleasure or satisfaction as before?

I think so? I mean, when I’m actually there, like sitting at the table and we’re joking around, I can laugh and get into it. I don’t usually sit there thinking, “This isn’t fun.”

It’s more before and after that my head gets busy. Like I’ll be watching the clock or thinking about what I didn’t finish, and then I get distracted. But the actual thing… I don’t know, I think I still enjoy it. It’s just not as simple as it used to feel.
After you go out and participate in something you enjoy, like trivia night, do you usually feel energized or do you tend to feel more drained afterward than you used to?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, sometimes I come home tired, but then… I also think anyone would be tired if they were out after work, right?

Like with trivia, if I go, I’ll usually be glad I went. But afterward I might be thinking about the next morning, or whether I stayed too late, or I’ll start doing that thing where I replay something I said—actually, sorry, that’s not exactly what you asked.

Energized versus drained… I don’t know. I haven’t really paid attention to whether it’s different than before. I guess I’d say I can feel tired after, but I don’t know if that’s more than it used to be.
Over the past two weeks, have you found yourself feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, even when there wasn’t an obvious reason like stress at work?

I don’t know if I’d call it depressed most of the day, nearly every day. I mean, I have days where I’m kind of low or just worn out, but it’s hard for me to separate that from everything else going on.

Like, sometimes I’ll wake up and already be thinking about the day before I’ve even gotten out of bed, and then I’m in this mood, but I don’t know if that’s “down” exactly. It’s not like I’m sitting around crying all day or anything.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed most of the day for two weeks straight. At least not in a way that feels separate from being stressed or overwhelmed.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt fatigued or lost your energy nearly every day, even when you haven’t been particularly busy or stressed?

I’m not sure I can say “nearly every day.” I do feel tired a lot, but then I start thinking, well, maybe that’s just because I didn’t sleep great, or because work takes a lot out of me, or because I had too much coffee and then crashed later.

Even on quieter days, I might feel kind of low-energy, but I don’t really track it that closely. Like, I’ll sit down after work and suddenly it’s two hours later and I haven’t done the laundry, but then I think maybe I was just avoiding it because I hate laundry. So… I don’t know. I’ve noticed being tired, but I’m not sure it’s nearly every day or for no reason.
Over the past two weeks, have you found it harder to focus, make decisions, or think clearly nearly every day, even when you’re not particularly stressed?

I’m not sure. I mean, I definitely have moments where I feel like I’m rereading the same email three times or I can’t decide what to make for dinner, but then I think… isn’t that kind of normal?

At work, there are so many little decisions all day, and by the time I get home I’ll stand in front of the fridge like it’s some huge problem, which is ridiculous. But I don’t know if that’s “nearly every day,” or if it’s happening when I’m not stressed. I feel like I’m usually at least a little stressed, so it’s hard to separate.

So I guess… I’ve noticed some trouble focusing or deciding things, but I can’t really say clearly that it’s been nearly every day for no reason.
Have you noticed that you don’t get as much pleasure or satisfaction out of things as you used to—even if you still enjoy them a little?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I still like things when I’m doing them, I think. Like if I watch a show I like or get food from a place I’ve been craving, it’s not like I feel nothing.

But then sometimes I’ll plan to do something that sounds nice, and by the time it comes around I’m kind of… eh, about it. Although that also happens when the parking is annoying, or if I’ve had one of those days where every client seems to need something at the exact same time. Sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking.

I guess I haven’t clearly noticed that I don’t enjoy things anymore. It’s more that I sometimes don’t get myself to start them, if that makes sense.
Do you find that your worries or anxiety feel uncontrollable — like even when you try to focus on something else, your mind keeps going back to the things you’re worried about?

Yeah… that part, yes. I can try to tell myself, like, “Brenda, you already made the plan, you’ve thought through this, just let it go,” and for a few minutes I’ll think I’m fine.

But then I’ll be doing something else—answering an email or even just trying to watch something—and suddenly I’m back in it again. Like I check one concern off in my head, and then three more show up right behind it. It’s kind of like when my inbox looks manageable for half a second and then suddenly there are ten new things, except it’s just in my brain.

So yes, I guess it does feel hard to control. I don’t always realize I’ve gone back to worrying until I’m already deep in another loop.
Have you noticed yourself feeling physically restless, like you can't sit still, or like you're keyed up inside, even when you're not actively trying to sleep?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not always like I’m pacing around the room or anything, but inside I feel really wound up a lot of the time.

Like, I’ll be home eating dinner and my body feels like I’m still sitting in a pipeline review, waiting for someone to ask me something I should already know the answer to. Which is silly, because I’m just at my kitchen table, and half the time I’m just trying to eat whatever leftovers I found. And my shoulders—this is probably related—my shoulders are tight constantly. I’ll notice them up near my ears and try to drop them, and then five minutes later they’re right back up again.

So yes, I guess “keyed up” is a good way to put it. It’s like I don’t fully settle down, even when there isn’t anything happening right that second.
Do you ever feel like even when you do sleep, you still wake up feeling tired or like you didn’t really rest well?

Yeah. That’s actually a big part of why I’m here, honestly. My sleep has gotten really unreliable.

I’ll go to bed completely exhausted, like I should just pass out, but then I’m lying there replaying forecast numbers or something that happened with my team, or worrying about whether I handled a client issue the right way. And then if I do fall asleep, I’ll wake up around 3 or 4 in the morning and it’s like my brain immediately turns back on.

It’s frustrating because I’ll think, “Okay, you’re tired, just sleep,” but then I’m mentally back at work, which is ridiculous because it’s dark and nothing can even be done about it then. So yeah, even when I technically slept, I wake up feeling like I didn’t really get rest.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent and excessive worry across multiple domains, difficulty controlling anxiety, sleep disturbance, and somatic symptoms (e.g., muscle tension, restlessness), consistent with generalized anxiety disorder. Depressive symptoms are not sufficiently pervasive or persistent to meet criteria for a major depressive episode.
